title: Syllabus
text:
Welcome to DATASCI 151! This Maymester course introduces data analysis and statistical computing with Python and SQL. It is designed for beginners, so you do not need any programming experience to take it.
We will cover the basics of Python programming, Jupyter Notebooks for reproducible research, data wrangling and merging with SQL, and data visualisation.
You will work with real datasets and problems throughout the course and use these tools to answer questions with data. The course builds your technical skills and your critical thinking, which you will need for any data analysis you do later on.

title: Jupyter Notebook and Markdown
text:
This tutorial introduces Jupyter Notebook and Markdown. Jupyter Notebook lets you write documents that mix live code, equations, plots and text. Markdown is a simple way to format text, and people use it for websites, notes, books, presentations, emails and technical documentation. WhatsApp uses a similar syntax too, so if you have ever made a word bold or italic on WhatsApp, you have already used something very close to Markdown!
The tutorial has two parts. The first part shows you how to create a notebook, run code cells and write text cells. The second part covers Markdown in more detail: headings, lists, tables, equations, figures and footnotes.

title: Jupyter Notebook and Markdown
text:
What is Jupyter Notebook?
Jupyter Notebook is free, open-source software for writing documents that combine code, equations, plots and text. It supports over 40 programming languages, including Python, R and Julia, and it is very popular in data science, machine learning and scientific computing.
A notebook is made of cells. Each cell contains either code or text, and when you run a code cell you see the result right below it. You can run one cell at a time or the whole notebook. Notebooks are saved as .ipynb files, which you can share with others so they can reproduce your analysis.

title: Jupyter Notebook and Markdown
text:
Creating a new notebook
First, please make sure you have Anaconda and VS Code installed on your computer. If you have not installed them yet, Tutorial 01 shows you how.
To create a new notebook in VS Code, go to “File” > “New File”. A prompt will appear in the middle of the screen. Select “Jupyter Notebook”.



Creating a new Jupyter Notebook in VS Code.


VS Code will create a new notebook with the .ipynb extension. You can give it a name when you save it. An empty notebook looks like this:



An empty Jupyter Notebook.


Please do not forget to select the Python version the notebook should use (Jupyter calls it the “kernel”). Click on “Select Kernel” at the top right corner of the screen and choose Anaconda’s “base” environment.



Selecting the Python interpreter for the notebook.


To add a code cell, click on “+ Code”. You will see an empty grey box with “Python” in the lower-right corner. Type your Python code in the box and run it by clicking on the “Run” button on its left, or by pressing Shift + Enter.



A code cell in a Jupyter Notebook.


For example, type the following code in the cell:

print("Welcome to DATASCI 151!")

x = 5
y = 10
z = x + y
print(z)

The result appears right below the cell:



Output of the code cell.


To add a text cell, click on “+ Markdown”. You will get an empty box where you can type text. We will see Markdown in more detail in the next section, but for now, type the following text in the cell:
# Welcome to DATASCI 151!

This is a Jupyter Notebook. You can write *text*, **equations**, and `code` 
in [this notebook](https://github.com/danilofreire/datasci151-summer/blob/main/tutorials/testing-ipython.ipynb). 
The text cell will look like this:



A text cell in a Jupyter Notebook.


Run the text cell with the tick button or Shift + Enter. The first block in the image shows the text before you run the cell, and the second block shows it after. To edit the text again, just double-click on it.

title: Jupyter Notebook and Markdown
text:
Why use Markdown?
Markdown is simple, easy to learn and supported almost everywhere. With a few symbols you can add headings, lists, tables, equations and figures to your documents. Jupyter Notebook, GitHub and Slack all use Markdown, so you will use what you learn here in many other places.

title: Jupyter Notebook and Markdown
text:
Headings
Use the # symbol for headings. # Heading 1 creates a first-level heading, ## Heading 2 a second-level heading, and so on, up to six levels.
# Heading 1
## Heading 2
### Heading 3

title: Jupyter Notebook and Markdown
text:
Lists
This is how you write a numbered list with bullet points inside it:
1. This is an ordered list.
2. This is the second item in the ordered list.
  - This is a sub-item in the unordered list.
    - This is a sub-sub-item in the unordered list.

This is an ordered list.
This is the second item in the ordered list.

This is a sub-item in the unordered list.

This is a sub-sub-item in the unordered list.



And this is a bullet-point list:
- This is an unordered list.
- This is the second item in the unordered list.
  - This is a sub-item in the unordered list.

This is an unordered list.
This is the second item in the unordered list.

This is a sub-item in the unordered list.

title: Jupyter Notebook and Markdown
text:
Tables
Use the | symbol to separate the columns of a table. For example:
Table: Your Caption 

| A            | New              | Table          |
|:-------------|:----------------:|---------------:|
|left-aligned  |centre-aligned    |right-aligned   |
|*italics*     |~~strikethrough~~ |**boldface**    |

Your Caption

The colons in the second row set the alignment of each column. A colon on the left (:---) aligns the text to the left, colons on both sides (:---:) centre it, and a colon on the right (---:) aligns it to the right.

title: Jupyter Notebook and Markdown Tutorial
section: Creating Markdown Tables from Pandas DataFrames in Jupyter Notebooks
text:
Creating Markdown Tables from Pandas DataFrames in Jupyter Notebooks
When working with pandas DataFrames, you can convert them into Markdown tables for better presentation. The method is also relatively simple. Here is how to do it:

Prerequisites
Ensure you have the following installed:

Jupyter Notebook
pandas
tabulate (for enhanced table formatting)

Jupyter Notebook and pandas are included in the Anaconda distribution. You can install tabulate using conda install in your terminal. If you are using VS Code, you can open a terminal by clicking on “Terminal” > “New Terminal” in the top menu. Then run the following command:
conda install tabulate


Basic Method: Using pandas.DataFrame.to_markdown()
pandas provides a built-in method to_markdown() for converting DataFrames to Markdown tables.

Step 1: Import pandas and create a DataFrame
You can create a dataframe by passing a dictionary to the pd.DataFrame() constructor:

# If necessary, install pandas and tabulate 
# You should have pandas installed if you installed Anaconda, 
# but if you do not, you can install both with the following terminal command:
# conda install pandas tabulate

# Import pandas
import pandas as pd
from tabulate import tabulate

# Create a sample DataFrame
data = {
    "Name": ["Alice", "Bob", "Charlie"],
    "Age": [25, 30, 35],
    "City": ["New York", "London", "Paris"]
}
df = pd.DataFrame(data)



Step 2: Convert DataFrame to Markdown
Then you just need to call the to_markdown() method on the DataFrame:

# Print the DataFrame as a Markdown table, excluding the index
markdown_table = df.to_markdown(index=False)
print(markdown_table)

This will output:
| Name    | Age  | City     |
|:--------|-----:|:---------|
| Alice   |   25 | New York |
| Bob     |   30 | London   |
| Charlie |   35 | Paris    |


Step 3: Display in Jupyter Notebook
To display the Markdown table in a Jupyter Notebook cell, use the display() function from the IPython.display module:

# You should also have the IPython package installed if you installed Anaconda
# If not, you can install it with
# conda install ipython

# Import the Markdown display class. 
# This is what allows us to display Markdown in Jupyter Notebooks 
from IPython.display import display, Markdown

# Display the Markdown table
display(Markdown(markdown_table))

This will render a nicely formatted table in your notebook:



Markdown table in a Jupyter Notebook.





Advanced Formatting
You can customise the Markdown table using various parameters of to_markdown():

# Customising the Markdown table using the to_markdown() method
markdown_table = df.to_markdown(
    index=False,  # Don't include index
    tablefmt="pipe",  # Use pipe format
    floatfmt=".2f",  # Format floats to 2 decimal places
    headers=["Name", "Age (Years)", "City"],  # Custom headers
    colalign=("left", "center", "right")  # Align columns
)
display(Markdown(markdown_table))



Using tabulate for Enhanced Formatting
The tabulate library offers even more formatting options. While they are not necessary for basic tables, they can be useful for more complex tables. In our course, you will probably not need them, but I will show you how to use them for your reference. Please check their documentation for more information.

from tabulate import tabulate

markdown_table = tabulate(df, headers='keys', tablefmt='pipe', showindex=False)
display(Markdown(markdown_table))



Best Practices

Index: Consider whether you need the index in your table. Often, it is cleaner to exclude it using index=False.
Formatting: Use floatfmt to control decimal places for numerical data.
Headers: Customize headers for clarity, especially if your DataFrame column names are not user-friendly.
Table Format: Experiment with different tablefmt options to find the most suitable for your needs.
Large DataFrames: For large DataFrames, consider displaying only a subset of rows or columns to maintain readability.



Example: Comprehensive Table Creation
Here is a more comprehensive example incorporating various best practices:

# Import necessary packages
import pandas as pd
from IPython.display import display, Markdown
from tabulate import tabulate

# Create a sample DataFrame
data = {
    "Product": ["Laptop", "Smartphone", "Tablet"],
    "Price": [999.99, 599.50, 299.75],
    "Stock": [50, 100, 75],
    "Rating": [4.5, 4.8, 4.2]
}
df = pd.DataFrame(data)

# Create a formatted Markdown table
markdown_table = tabulate(
    df,
    headers=["Product Name", "Price ($)", "Stock Quantity", "Customer Rating"],
    tablefmt="pipe", # Format as Markdown table
    floatfmt=(".2f", ".2f", "d", ".1f"),
    showindex=False, # Don't show the index (row numbers)
    numalign="right", # Align numbers to the right
    stralign="left" # Align strings (text, first column) to the left
)

# Display the table in the notebook
display(Markdown("### Product Inventory Summary"))
display(Markdown(markdown_table))

This will produce a well-formatted table with custom headers, appropriate number formatting, and a title.



Comprehensive Markdown table in a Jupyter Notebook.

title: Jupyter Notebook and Markdown
text:
Equations
Write equations between two $$ symbols. For example, here is the formula for the standard deviation of a population:
$$
\sigma = \sqrt{\frac{\sum_{i=1}^{N} (x_i - \mu)^2}{N}}
$$
\[
\sigma = \sqrt{\frac{\sum_{i=1}^{N} (x_i - \mu)^2}{N}}
\]
For an equation inside a sentence, use a single $. For example, $\alpha = \beta + \gamma$ becomes \(\alpha = \beta + \gamma\). Equations use LaTeX syntax, and the Overleaf documentation lists the symbols you can use.

title: Jupyter Notebook and Markdown
text:
Figures
To add a figure, use the ![Caption](path/to/image.png) syntax. For example:
![This is a figure caption.](path/to/image.png)
This adds the image path/to/image.png to your document, with the caption “This is a figure caption.”
Plots you create with Python appear automatically below the code cell that makes them.

title: Jupyter Notebook and Markdown
text:
Citations
Tools such as Quarto can create citations automatically from BibTeX files, but there is no reliable way to do this in Jupyter Notebooks. The two packages I know, cite2c and JupyterLab Citation Manager, are not ideal: the first has not been maintained for years, and the second is not ready for most uses. So I suggest you copy each citation from Google Scholar and paste it into a Markdown cell called “References” at the end of your notebook. You can write inline citations by hand too, such as “(McKinney, 2022)”.

I will post the assignments in the assignments/ folder as the course goes on, and each quiz will have its own GitHub repository. I will also announce them in class and on Canvas. The syllabus and the lecture schedule have all due dates and submission guidelines.


Tutorials
The Tutorials page has step-by-step guides for the tools we use in the course. Please have a look at them before our first class, as they will help you get started.

You can run Python directly in your browser at https://danilofreire.github.io/datasci151-summer/jupyter, with no installation required. It runs on Pyodide, a version of Python for the browser that comes with pandas, numpy, matplotlib and the other libraries we use in the course. It is useful for quick experiments when you do not have Anaconda at hand.

title: Jupyter Notebook and Markdown
section: Creating Markdown tables from pandas DataFrames
text:
Creating Markdown tables from pandas DataFrames
You can also turn a pandas DataFrame into a Markdown table, which often looks nicer in a report. Here is how to do it.

Prerequisites
You will need:

Jupyter Notebook
pandas
tabulate (for enhanced table formatting)

Jupyter Notebook and pandas come with Anaconda. You can install tabulate with conda install in the terminal. In VS Code, open a terminal by clicking on “Terminal” > “New Terminal” in the top menu, then run:
conda install tabulate


The basic method: pandas.DataFrame.to_markdown()
pandas has a built-in method, to_markdown(), that converts a DataFrame into a Markdown table.

Step 1: import pandas and create a DataFrame
Create a DataFrame by passing a dictionary to pd.DataFrame():

# If necessary, install pandas and tabulate 
# You should have pandas installed if you installed Anaconda, 
# but if you do not, you can install both with the following terminal command:
# conda install pandas tabulate

# Import pandas
import pandas as pd
from tabulate import tabulate

# Create a sample DataFrame
data = {
    "Name": ["Alice", "Bob", "Charlie"],
    "Age": [25, 30, 35],
    "City": ["New York", "London", "Paris"]
}
df = pd.DataFrame(data)



Step 2: convert the DataFrame to Markdown
Then call to_markdown() on the DataFrame:

# Print the DataFrame as a Markdown table, excluding the index
markdown_table = df.to_markdown(index=False)
print(markdown_table)

This will output:
| Name    | Age  | City     |
|:--------|-----:|:---------|
| Alice   |   25 | New York |
| Bob     |   30 | London   |
| Charlie |   35 | Paris    |


Step 3: display the table in the notebook
To show the table as formatted Markdown, use the display() function from the IPython.display module:

# You should also have the IPython package installed if you installed Anaconda
# If not, you can install it with
# conda install ipython

# Import the Markdown display class. 
# This is what allows us to display Markdown in Jupyter Notebooks 
from IPython.display import display, Markdown

# Display the Markdown table
display(Markdown(markdown_table))

The notebook will show a formatted table:



Markdown table in a Jupyter Notebook.





More formatting options
to_markdown() has several arguments that change how the table looks:

# Customising the Markdown table using the to_markdown() method
markdown_table = df.to_markdown(
    index=False,  # Don't include index
    tablefmt="pipe",  # Use pipe format
    floatfmt=".2f",  # Format floats to 2 decimal places
    headers=["Name", "Age (Years)", "City"],  # Custom headers
    colalign=("left", "center", "right")  # Align columns
)
display(Markdown(markdown_table))



Using tabulate
The tabulate library has even more formatting options. You will probably not need them in our course, but I include an example here in case you want to try them. Please see the tabulate documentation for more information.

from tabulate import tabulate

markdown_table = tabulate(df, headers='keys', tablefmt='pipe', showindex=False)
display(Markdown(markdown_table))



Tips

You often do not need the index (the row numbers), so remove it with index=False
Use floatfmt to set the number of decimal places
Rename the headers if your column names are hard to read
Try different tablefmt options to see which one you like best
For large DataFrames, show only some of the rows or columns so the table stays readable



A complete example
Here is an example that uses several of these tips:

# Import necessary packages
import pandas as pd
from IPython.display import display, Markdown
from tabulate import tabulate

# Create a sample DataFrame
data = {
    "Product": ["Laptop", "Smartphone", "Tablet"],
    "Price": [999.99, 599.50, 299.75],
    "Stock": [50, 100, 75],
    "Rating": [4.5, 4.8, 4.2]
}
df = pd.DataFrame(data)

# Create a formatted Markdown table
markdown_table = tabulate(
    df,
    headers=["Product Name", "Price ($)", "Stock Quantity", "Customer Rating"],
    tablefmt="pipe", # Format as Markdown table
    floatfmt=(".2f", ".2f", "d", ".1f"),
    showindex=False, # Don't show the index (row numbers)
    numalign="right", # Align numbers to the right
    stralign="left" # Align strings (text, first column) to the left
)

# Display the table in the notebook
display(Markdown("### Product Inventory Summary"))
display(Markdown(markdown_table))

The result is a table with a title, custom headers and formatted numbers.



Comprehensive Markdown table in a Jupyter Notebook.

title: The terminal and conda environments
text:
This tutorial shows you how to use the terminal in VS Code to run conda commands, and how to create and manage Python environments. Please do Tutorial 01 first, as you will need VS Code and Anaconda installed. We also cover environments in Lecture 02, so you can use this tutorial as a reference after class.
In this course we will use Anaconda’s default environment, base, so creating your own environments is optional. But environments are very useful once you start working on more than one project, and it is good to know how they work.

title: The terminal and conda environments
text:
macOS
On macOS, the terminal uses a program called zsh. The first time you use conda, run these two commands:
conda init zsh
conda update conda
Then close the terminal and open it again. From now on, you can type conda commands directly. If you see conda: command not found, please check that Anaconda finished installing and then run conda init zsh again.

title: The terminal and conda environments
text:
Windows
On Windows, VS Code may open PowerShell or Command Prompt by default, and these may not find conda. Please switch to the Anaconda PowerShell Prompt instead:

Click on the small arrow next to the + icon at the top of the terminal panel
Select “Anaconda PowerShell Prompt” from the list

If you do not see it in the list, you can also open the “Anaconda PowerShell Prompt” from the Windows Start menu. Anaconda’s guide to VS Code has more details.

title: The terminal and conda environments
text:
Check that conda works
Type the following command and press Enter:
conda --version
You should see something like conda 25.x.x. The exact number does not matter.

title: The terminal and conda environments
text:
Create an environment
This command creates a new environment called datasci151 with Python 3.12:
conda create -n datasci151 python=3.12 -y

conda create creates a new environment
-n datasci151 sets its name (-n is short for --name)
python=3.12 says which Python version to install

title: The terminal and conda environments
text:
Activate the environment
To use the environment, you need to activate it:
conda activate datasci151
The name of the active environment appears in brackets at the start of the terminal line, for example (datasci151). Every conda install command now installs packages into this environment.

title: The terminal and conda environments
text:
Install packages
Install the packages we use in the course:
conda install numpy pandas matplotlib jupyter -y
To remove a package, use conda remove package_name.

title: The terminal and conda environments
text:
List your environments
To see all your environments, run:
conda env list
The active environment has an asterisk (*) next to it.

title: The terminal and conda environments
text:
Deactivate the environment
When you finish, go back to base with:
conda deactivate

title: The terminal and conda environments
text:
Delete an environment
If you no longer need an environment, you can delete it with:
conda remove -n datasci151 --all -y
Please be careful, as this deletes the environment and all its packages. Your own files (notebooks, scripts, datasets) are not affected.

title: Installing SQLite and SQLite3 Editor
text:
In Lectures 11 to 13, we will use SQL to work with databases. This tutorial helps you set up everything you need before Lecture 11, so we can start writing queries right away in class. Please do Tutorial 01 first, as you will need VS Code and Anaconda installed.
You will set up three things:

The sqlite3 module in Python, which comes with Anaconda, so you only need to check that it works
The SQLite3 Editor extension for VS Code, which lets you see and edit databases without writing code
The sqlite3 command-line tool (optional), which lets you run SQL in the terminal

title: Installing SQLite and SQLite3 Editor
text:
Create your first database
Let us check that the extension works:

In VS Code, click on “File” > “New File” and save the file as example.db
Click on example.db in the file explorer on the left. VS Code will open it with SQLite3 Editor




An empty database in SQLite3 Editor


If VS Code opens the file as text instead, right-click on example.db, select “Open With…” and choose “SQLite3 Editor”.
Now type the following query in the editor’s query box at the bottom and run it:
CREATE TABLE students (
    id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY,
    name TEXT,
    age INTEGER
);
You should see a new, empty table called students. That is all you need for Lecture 11!

title: Installing SQLite and SQLite3 Editor
text:
macOS
SQLite comes with macOS. Open a terminal and type:
sqlite3 --version
You should see a version number. To open the SQLite prompt, type sqlite3. To leave it, type .quit and press Enter.

title: Installing SQLite and SQLite3 Editor
text:
Windows
The easiest way is to install SQLite with conda. Open the Anaconda PowerShell Prompt and run:
conda install sqlite -y
Anaconda may already include it, in which case conda will tell you that there is nothing to install. Then check that it works:
sqlite3 --version
To open the SQLite prompt, type sqlite3. To leave it, type .quit and press Enter.
You can also download SQLite from the official website, but then you have to add it to your system’s PATH yourself, so I recommend the conda option.

title: Installing SQLite and SQLite3 Editor
text:
Linux
Most Linux distributions include SQLite. If yours does not, install the sqlite3 package with your package manager, for example sudo apt install sqlite3 on Ubuntu.
